title: AOS-Bench: Can LLM Agents Manage Dynamic Workloads?
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence
  [Submitted on 23 Oct 2026]
Title:AOS-Bench: Can LLM Agents Manage Dynamic Workloads?
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Coding agents are moving from handling one request at a time to serving as persistent assistants to which users hand a stream of work: a build, a data-processing job and a bug fix may all be pending on the same machine at once. Such an agent must decide when to take on new tasks, how to delegate and overlap them, and how to stay within the machine's CPU and memory. Existing benchmarks cannot measure this, because they evaluate each task in isolation. We introduce \benchname{}, which evaluates an agent system as a workload manager: verified tasks arrive over time and must be delivered under shared CPU and memory limits, and the same tasks run one at a time serve as a per-system reference.
Across five model--harness pairs, isolated task success does not carry over evenly. On heavy workloads every system loses 13 to 23 points. On medium workloads, systems span 11 points in isolated success but 26 points in stream success, and two systems 0.6 points apart in isolation deliver 54\% and 68\% of the same tasks. Execution-policy interventions trace much of this gap to task intake: serial dispatch leaves 73\% of heavy-workload tasks unclaimed. Yet more elaborate management does not necessarily help. A fixed concurrency of two comes within four points of the best agent-managed policy on both medium and heavy workloads, and under every policy median CPU use stays below 30\% of the provisioned cores while tasks wait. These results identify workload management as a distinct capability for agents, and \benchname{} as a way to measure it.

report.summary: A new benchmark, AOS-Bench, shows that LLM coding agents good at one-off tasks often fail as persistent workload managers juggling concurrent jobs under shared CPU and memory limits.
report.background: Coding agents have evolved from single-shot assistants into persistent systems that users hand a continuous stream of work: a build here, a data-processing job there, a bug fix queued behind them, all on one machine. Existing benchmarks such as SWE-bench and Terminal-Bench evaluate tasks in isolation, one at a time, so they cannot capture the scheduling, delegation and resource-contention decisions that dominate real deployments. AOS-Bench was built to close that gap: verified tasks arrive over time and must be completed under shared CPU and memory caps, with the same tasks run serially acting as a per-system baseline. The authors tested five model–harness combinations to see whether isolated task success predicts performance under a live, streamed workload.
key_points: Isolated success does not transfer. On heavy workloads every tested system lost 13 to 23 percentage points versus its serial baseline, meaning a strong single-task agent can still drop a large share of work once jobs overlap.

Rankings reshuffle under load. On medium workloads systems spanned 11 points in isolated success but 26 points in streamed success; two systems only 0.6 points apart in isolation delivered 54% and 68% of the same task stream.
Task intake is the main bottleneck. Policy experiments trace much of the gap to dispatch: a serial policy left 73% of heavy-workload tasks unclaimed, because the agent never picked them up in time.

Smarter management is not automatically better. A simple fixed concurrency of two came within four points of the best agent-managed policy on both medium and heavy workloads, suggesting elaborate scheduling logic adds little.

Resources were not the constraint. Under every policy, median CPU use stayed below 30% of provisioned cores while tasks waited, pointing to decision-making rather than hardware capacity as the limiting factor.
report.impact: The paper reframes workload management as a distinct agent capability rather than a byproduct of coding skill, which matters for how the industry evaluates and markets agents. For developers, it argues that harness design, queueing and dispatch policy deserve as much attention as model choice, and that a simple concurrency cap may beat complex orchestration. For benchmark authors, it exposes a blind spot: leaderboard scores from isolated tasks can mispredict production behavior badly enough to invert rankings. For end users and teams deploying persistent assistants, the practical takeaway is that idle CPU and dropped tasks may signal scheduling failures, so vendors should report streamed, multi-job performance alongside single-task results.
report.tools: Watch for the AOS-Bench harness and task suite if released alongside the paper. To explore the same problem, combine agent orchestration frameworks (LangGraph, AutoGen, CrewAI, Ray) with OS-level resource controls such as cgroups v2, Docker memory/CPU limits and systemd slices. Adjacent benchmarks worth reading include SWE-bench, Terminal-Bench and OSWorld, plus queueing tools like Celery or Kubernetes job controllers for concurrency-policy experiments.
